definition: A test that records the electrical signals of the heart to check for rhythm problems or heart attacks.
An ultrasound of the heart that produces moving pictures of heart valves, chambers, and pumping strength.
The pressure of circulating blood against the walls of blood vessels, recorded as systolic over diastolic (e.g. 120/80 mmHg).
Persistently high blood pressure (consistently >= 140/90 mmHg).
Narrowing or blockage of coronary arteries usually caused by atherosclerosis (plaque buildup).
Heart attack; occurs when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is severely blocked, causing muscle damage.
A serious, classic heart attack where an artery is completely blocked, visible as ST elevation on ECG.
A heart attack where the artery is partially blocked; detected by elevated cardiac enzymes without ST elevation.
Condition where the heart is unable to pump blood efficiently to meet the body's needs.
Percentage of blood leaving your heart's left ventricle each time it contracts (normal is 50% to 70%).
An irregular, often very rapid heart rhythm that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure.
Open heart bypass surgery to redirect blood around clogged arteries using healthy blood vessels from elsewhere in the body.
Minimally invasive procedure (angioplasty) using a balloon and stent to open clogged heart arteries.
Chest pain or pressure caused by reduced blood flow to heart muscle.
Any abnormality or disturbance in the regular rhythm of the heartbeat.
Abnormally slow resting heart rate (typically below 60 beats per minute).
Abnormally rapid resting heart rate (typically above 100 beats per minute).
Sensations of a racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping heartbeat.
A blood clot that forms in a deep vein, most commonly in the legs or calves.
A life-threatening blockage in the pulmonary arteries of the lungs, often caused by a blood clot traveling from the legs.
A protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, used to diagnose a heart attack.
A hormone released by heart ventricles under stretch and strain, elevated in heart failure.
A wearable portable ECG device that continuously records heart electrical activity for 24 to 48 hours.
An exercise ECG test monitoring heart activity while walking or running on a treadmill.
A small surgically implanted electronic device that sends electrical pulses to keep the heart beating at a normal rate.
A progressive inflammatory lung disease that causes obstructed airflow from the lungs (includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis).
A chronic inflammatory condition where airways narrow, swell, and produce extra mucus, causing wheezing and breathlessness.
The percentage of oxygen-saturated hemoglobin in the blood, measured with a pulse oximeter (normal 95-100%).
A quick projectional radiograph of the chest used to diagnose pneumonia, pneumothorax, and heart enlargement.
Breathing tests (spirometry) that measure how much air your lungs can hold and how quickly you can blow it out.
Severe, life-threatening inflammatory lung condition causing fluid buildup in alveoli and profound oxygen deficit.
A blood test drawn from an artery measuring oxygen, carbon dioxide levels, and arterial blood pH balance.
A sleep disorder where throat muscles intermittently relax and block the airway during sleep, causing loud snoring and pauses in breathing.
Inhalation of food, liquid, or stomach contents into the lungs, which can cause chemical pneumonitis or aspiration pneumonia.
Inflammation of the lining of the bronchial tubes, which carry air to and from the lungs.
A collapsed lung occurring when air leaks into the space between the lung and chest wall.
Excess buildup of fluid between the layers of the pleura outside the lungs.
Coughing up blood or blood-stained mucus from the respiratory tract.
Difficult or labored breathing; shortness of breath.
Difficulty breathing that worsens when lying flat, often relieved by propping up with pillows (classic sign of heart failure).
A high-pitched wheezing sound caused by disrupted airflow through a narrowed upper airway (larynx or trachea).
A continuous, high-pitched whistling sound produced during breathing out through narrowed airways.
Non-invasive respiratory support devices that deliver pressurized air through a mask to keep airways open.
Stroke; damage to the brain from interrupted blood supply (ischemic) or ruptured blood vessel (hemorrhagic).
A temporary period of stroke-like symptoms that resolves within 24 hours without permanent damage ('mini-stroke').
A test that detects and records electrical activity in your brain using small metal discs (electrodes) attached to the scalp.
The pressure exerted by fluids such as cerebrospinal fluid inside the skull and on the brain tissue.
A 15-point neurological scale used to assess a person's level of consciousness (eye, verbal, motor responses).
A chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers.
A progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting motor nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord (motor neuron disease).
A progressive nervous system disorder affecting movement, causing resting tremors, muscle stiffness, and slowed motion.
A central nervous system neurological disorder in which brain activity becomes abnormal, causing recurring seizures.
Weakness, numbness, and burning pain from nerve damage, usually in the hands and feet (common in diabetes).
Any diffuse disease of the brain that alters brain function or mental state (e.g., hepatic or metabolic encephalopathy).
Inability or difficulty speaking, understanding speech, reading, or writing, usually following stroke or brain trauma.
Lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements, leading to an unsteady, clumsy gait or clumsy speech.
Temporary loss of consciousness caused by a sudden fall in blood pressure to the brain; fainting.
A false sensation that you or your environment is spinning, spinning dizziness, often due to inner ear disturbances.
Inflammation of the protective membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord, typically caused by bacterial or viral infection.
Procedure where a needle is inserted between two lower back vertebrae to sample cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
A group of metabolic diseases characterized by elevated blood glucose levels resulting from defects in insulin secretion or action.
Autoimmune condition where pancreatic beta cells are destroyed, producing little or no insulin.
Chronic condition where the body becomes resistant to insulin or doesn't produce enough insulin.
A blood test showing average blood sugar levels over the past 2 to 3 months (normal <5.7%, diabetes >=6.5%).
Blood glucose level measured after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours (normal 70-99 mg/dL).
Blood glucose level measured exactly 2 hours after a meal (normal <140 mg/dL).
Blood sugar tested at any random time regardless of meals.
A life-threatening complication of diabetes where lack of insulin forces the body to burn fat for fuel, producing toxic acidic ketones.
A severe metabolic complication of type 2 diabetes with extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL) and dehydration without prominent ketoacidosis.
Abnormally low blood sugar level (<70 mg/dL), causing shaking, sweating, confusion, and dizziness.
A pituitary hormone that regulates the thyroid gland; high TSH indicates underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), low indicates hyperthyroidism.
Primary hormones produced by the thyroid gland that regulate energy metabolism.
An underactive thyroid gland that does not produce enough thyroid hormones, causing fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance.
An overactive thyroid gland producing excess thyroid hormones, causing weight loss, rapid heartbeat, and anxiety.
A hormonal disorder causing enlarged ovaries with small cysts, irregular periods, excess androgen, and insulin resistance.
A condition caused by prolonged exposure to high levels of the hormone cortisol, leading to a round 'moon' face and abdominal weight gain.
A disorder where adrenal glands do not produce enough cortisol and aldosterone, causing low blood pressure, fatigue, and dark skin patches.
A sudden episode of kidney failure or kidney damage that happens within a few hours or days.
Long-term, gradual loss of kidney function over months or years.
A calculation showing how efficiently the kidneys filter waste from blood (normal >=90 mL/min/1.73m2; <15 indicates kidney failure).
A waste product from muscle breakdown filtered exclusively by kidneys; elevated levels signal reduced kidney clearance.
A waste product from protein breakdown; high levels indicate decreased kidney filtration or dehydration.
Infection in any part of the urinary system (kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra).
Presence of red blood cells in the urine (microscopic or visible red urine).
Abnormal leakage of proteins into urine, an early marker of kidney glomerulus damage.
Final stage of chronic kidney disease where kidneys have lost nearly all functioning capacity, requiring dialysis or kidney transplant.
A medical treatment where a machine filters waste, salts, and excess fluid from blood when kidneys fail.
A type of dialysis using the lining of your abdomen (peritoneal membrane) to filter blood inside the body.
Hard mineral and salt deposits that form inside the kidneys and cause severe flank pain when passing through the ureter.
Pain, discomfort, or burning sensation during urination.
Abnormally low production of urine (<400 mL/day in adults).
Non-passage of urine (<100 mL/day), a medical emergency signaling complete kidney shutdown or urinary obstruction.
Non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland in older men that squeezes the urethra and obstructs urine flow.
A protein produced by the prostate gland; elevated blood levels can indicate BPH, infection, or prostate cancer.
A digestive disorder where stomach acid repeatedly flows back up into the esophagus, causing heartburn.
A common functional gastrointestinal disorder causing cramping, abdominal pain, bloating, gas, and alternating diarrhea or constipation.
Chronic autoimmune inflammation of the digestive tract, including Crohn's disease and Ulcerative Colitis.
A type of IBD causing inflammation anywhere from the mouth to anus, often affecting the full thickness of bowel wall.
A chronic IBD that causes long-lasting inflammation and ulcers in the innermost lining of the large intestine (colon and rectum).
A panel of blood tests that measure liver enzymes (SGOT, SGPT, ALP), bilirubin, and proteins (albumin).
An enzyme found in liver and heart muscle cells; elevated in liver injury or myocardial damage.
A liver-specific enzyme that spills into blood when liver cells are inflamed or injured.
A yellowish pigment formed during normal breakdown of red blood cells; elevated levels cause jaundice.
Yellowish staining of the skin, whites of the eyes (sclerae), and mucous membranes caused by high levels of bilirubin.
Late-stage fibrosis (scarring) of the liver caused by many forms of liver diseases, such as chronic viral hepatitis or alcohol abuse.
Abnormal buildup of fluid in the abdominal peritoneal cavity, most often caused by liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
Inflammation of the liver tissue, most commonly viral or autoimmune.
Open sores that develop on the inside lining of your stomach (gastric ulcer) and upper small intestine (duodenal ulcer).
A spiral bacterium that infects the stomach lining, the leading cause of peptic ulcers and chronic gastritis.
A specialized endoscopic procedure used to examine and treat bile duct and pancreatic duct stones and strictures.
Hardened deposits of digestive fluid (cholesterol or bilirubin) that form inside the gallbladder.
Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by a gallstone blocking the cystic duct.
Inflammation of the pancreas gland; causes severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back.
Enzymes tested in blood to diagnose acute pancreatitis (Lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer).
Difficulty or painful sensation when swallowing food or liquids.
Vomiting of blood (bright red or dark 'coffee-ground' appearance), signaling upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
Dark, black, tarry, foul-smelling stools caused by digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed.
Passage of fresh bright red blood from the anus, usually signaling lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
A standard blood panel measuring red blood cells, white blood cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs throughout the body (normal: men 13.8-17.2, women 12.1-15.1 g/dL).

full_form: White Blood Cells / Total Leukocyte Count
definition: Immune cells that fight infection; elevated count indicates infection or inflammation.
Percentage breakdown of individual white blood cell types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.
Small cell fragments essential for normal blood clotting (normal 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter).
Abnormally low platelet count in blood (<150,000/uL), increasing the risk of bruising and bleeding.
Condition marked by a deficiency of red blood cells or hemoglobin, leading to fatigue, pallor, and weakness.
A standardized measurement of blood clotting time, used to monitor blood-thinning medications like Warfarin.
Test measuring how many seconds it takes for plasma to clot after addition of tissue thromboplastin.
A blood test characterizing coagulation and monitoring IV unfractionated heparin therapy.
Rate at which red blood cells sediment in a tube; a non-specific indicator of bodily inflammation.
A liver protein that surges rapidly in response to acute inflammation or bacterial infection in the body.
Surgical removal of a small sample of tissue or cells for examination under a microscope by a pathologist.
A non-cancerous growth that does not invade nearby tissue or spread to other parts of the body.
Cancerous cells that invade neighboring tissues and can spread (metastasize) to distant organs.
The spread of cancer cells from the primary site of origin to distant body organs via bloodstream or lymphatics.
The international standard system for classifying the extent and spread of malignant tumors.
Pharmacological treatment using chemical substances to destroy rapidly dividing cancer cells.
Treatment using high doses of targeted ionizing radiation to shrink tumors and destroy cancer cells.
A period during which the symptoms and detectable signs of a disease (such as cancer) decrease or disappear.
A life-threatening medical emergency caused by the body's extreme, dysregulated response to an infection, causing organ failure.
A profound subset of sepsis where circulatory and cellular abnormalities result in refractory low blood pressure and multi-organ failure.
Any biological agent (bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite) capable of causing disease in a host organism.
An infectious disease that jumps from non-human animals to humans (e.g. rabies, leptospirosis).
An infection acquired by a patient while receiving healthcare treatment in a hospital or clinic setting.
The time elapsed between exposure to a pathogen and the first appearance of clinical symptoms.
The constant, baseline presence or usual prevalence of a disease within a specific geographic area or population.
A sudden widespread increase in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population.
An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents, affecting a substantial portion of the global population.
Medication that destroys or slows down the growth of bacteria (ineffective against viral infections like common cold or flu).
Medication specifically designed to inhibit the replication of viruses (e.g. Oseltamivir, Acyclovir).
Medication used to treat fungal infections of skin, nails, or internal organs (e.g. Fluconazole).
A laboratory test where bacteria are grown from a body fluid sample and tested against different antibiotics to find the most effective drug.
The ability of bacteria and microbes to resist the effects of antibiotics that previously treated them, caused by overuse and misuse.
A molecular biology technique that amplifies tiny amounts of viral or bacterial DNA/RNA to diagnose infections with high precision.
A plate-based assay technique designed for detecting and quantifying soluble substances like antibodies or antigens.
A severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that develops within seconds or minutes of exposure to an allergen.
A common form of arthritis caused by the gradual breakdown of protective cartilage cushioning the ends of bones in joints.
A chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of joint membranes (synovium).
A bone disease that occurs when the body loses too much bone, making bones weak, brittle, and prone to fractures.
A low-dose imaging scan measuring bone mineral density to screen for osteopenia and osteoporosis.
A complete or partial break in the continuity of a bone.
An injury where bone ends are forcibly knocked or pulled out of their normal joint sockets.
Stretching or tearing of ligaments—the tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect two bones together in joints.
Stretching or tearing of muscle fibers or tendons—the fibrous cords of tissue that connect muscle to bone.
One of the key stabilizing ligaments in the center of the knee joint; often torn during sudden pivot motions in sports.
Orthopedic surgery to repair a severe bone fracture using plates, screws, pins, or rods to hold bones in alignment.
A painful form of inflammatory arthritis caused by high uric acid levels forming sharp urate crystals in joints (most often the big toe).
A waste product formed during the breakdown of purines in foods; elevated levels cause gout and uric acid kidney stones.
The first day of a woman's most recent menstrual bleeding, used to calculate gestational age and due dates.
The estimated date when spontaneous labor is expected to occur (40 weeks from the first day of LMP).
Routine medical and nursing care recommended for women during pregnancy to monitor maternal and fetal well-being.
Medical care given to the mother and newborn baby during the first six weeks following childbirth.
A surgical procedure used to deliver a baby through incisions in the mother's abdomen and uterus.
A pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in a fallopian tube (life-threatening emergency).
A serious pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and signs of damage to organ systems (protein in urine) after 20 weeks.
A condition in which pregnancy hormones cause elevated blood glucose levels in a pregnant mother.
A screening procedure for cervical cancer testing for precancerous cells on the cervix.
A common sexually transmitted virus; high-risk strains (HPV 16 and 18) cause the vast majority of cervical cancers.
An X-ray of the breast used to detect and diagnose breast cancer early.
A quick scoring system assessed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth to evaluate a newborn's physical condition (Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration).
The first nutrient-rich, antibody-dense breast milk produced in the first few days after delivery, essential for infant immunity.
India's national vaccination program providing free vaccines against 12 preventable diseases for infants and pregnant women.
The soft anatomical spots on an infant's skull where bone plates haven't yet fused (anterior fontanelle closes around 18 months).
As needed; taken only when necessary rather than on a fixed schedule (e.g. Paracetamol PRN for pain).
Immediately; given at once without delay (used for urgent emergency medications).
Medication to be taken once every 24 hours.
Medication to be taken twice a day, typically 12 hours apart.
Medication to be taken three times a day, typically every 8 hours.
Medication to be taken four times a day, typically every 6 hours.
Take if necessary / in case of need (similar to PRN).
By mouth / orally.
Nothing by mouth; patient must not eat or drink anything (fasting for surgery or test).
Administered directly into a vein through a catheter or needle.
Injected directly into a large muscle (e.g. deltoid or gluteus).
Injected into the fatty tissue layer just below the skin (e.g. insulin injections).
Dissolved under the tongue for rapid absorption into blood (e.g. nitroglycerin for angina).
Applied directly to a specific body surface (creams, ointments on skin, eye drops).
Medications that relieve pain, reduce inflammation, and lower fever without steroids (e.g. Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Diclofenac).
Medications that strongly decrease stomach acid secretion by blocking gastric proton pumps (e.g. Omeprazole, Pantoprazole).
Medications that inhibit blood clotting to prevent and treat clots (e.g. Heparin, Warfarin, Apixaban).
Medications that stop blood platelets from clumping together to prevent clots in arteries (e.g. Aspirin, Clopidogrel).
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitor; blood pressure and heart failure medication ending in '-pril' (e.g. Enalapril, Ramipril).
Blood pressure medication blocking angiotensin II receptors, ending in '-sartan' (e.g. Telmisartan, Losartan).
Medications that reduce heart rate and blood pressure by blocking adrenaline, ending in '-lol' (e.g. Metoprolol, Atenolol).
Medications that help the kidneys flush out excess water and salt through urine (e.g. Furosemide, Spironolactone).
Cholesterol-lowering medications that reduce heart attack and stroke risk (e.g. Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin).
A specific situation or condition in which a drug, procedure, or surgery should NOT be used because it may cause harm.
An unwanted, undesirable, or harmful effect that occurs after normal administration of a drug.
The strictest safety warning issued by drug regulatory authorities on a prescription drug's label regarding serious side effects.
The official, scientific chemical name of an active drug molecule (e.g. Paracetamol), as opposed to brand names (e.g. Crocin, Tylenol).
The time required for the concentration of a drug in the body or bloodstream to be reduced by half.
The process of gradually adjusting the dose of a medication upwards or downwards to achieve maximum benefit with minimal side effects.
Describing a disease or symptom with a sudden onset, sharp rise, and short duration.
Describing a condition or illness that persists over a long period (typically 3 months or more) and requires ongoing management.
The likely course, outcome, and chance of recovery from a disease.
The underlying cause, set of causes, or origin of a disease or medical condition.
Arising spontaneously or from an obscure or unknown cause.
Action, treatment, or medication taken to prevent a disease rather than treat an existing one.
Specialized medical care focused on relief from the symptoms, pain, and stress of a serious illness, prioritizing quality of life.
The sorting and prioritization of patients based on the urgency of their need for medical treatment.
The ability to walk independently or with assistive devices (early ambulation is encouraged after surgery).
Clinical measurements indicating state of bodily functions: Temperature, Pulse, Respiration rate, and Blood Pressure.
A flexible tube inserted through a narrow opening into a body cavity, duct, or vessel to drain fluids or administer fluids.
A thin tube inserted into a vein to administer fluids, medications, or blood products.
Listening to internal sounds of the body, usually using a stethoscope (lungs, heart, bowels).
Examining a part of the body by touching and feeling with hands to detect tenderness, size, shape, and firmness.
Tapping body parts with fingers or small instruments as part of a physical exam to evaluate tissue density and fluid presence.
Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in your body's tissues, commonly in feet, ankles, and legs.
Redness of the skin or mucous membranes caused by capillary congestion from injury or inflammation.
Containing or consisting of pus, usually indicating a bacterial infection.
The premature death of body cells or tissues through disease, injury, or severe blood supply failure.
Inadequate blood supply to an organ or part of the body, especially the heart muscles or brain.
Partial or complete loss of hair from where it normally grows; baldness.
Severe, uncomfortable itching sensation of the skin.
Temporary cessation or pause in breathing.
An abnormally low level of oxygen in arterial blood.
Excessive acidity of body fluids or tissues, marked by an abnormally low blood pH (<7.35).
Excessive alkalinity of body fluids or tissues, marked by an abnormally high blood pH (>7.45).
Presenting no clinical signs or symptoms of disease despite being infected or having the underlying condition.
Showing or exhibiting clinical symptoms of a condition or illness.
Administering nutrients or medications via routes outside the digestive tract (such as IV, IM, or SubQ injections).
Feeding or medication administration given directly into the gastrointestinal tract (oral or feeding tube).
Free from all living bacteria or other microorganisms.
Practices and procedures designed to prevent contamination from pathogens during clinical care.
A specialized hospital department providing intensive treatment and continuous monitoring for critically ill patients.
A hospital step-down care ward for patients who require more observation than a general ward but less than an intensive care unit.
The hospital section where patients receive diagnosis and consultation without staying overnight.
The hospital section where patients are formally admitted to a bed for treatment, monitoring, or surgery.
A sterile room in a hospital where surgical procedures are performed.
Recovery room where patients are closely monitored after surgery as they wake up from anesthesia.
A permanent identification number assigned to a patient linking all lifetime medical visits, tests, and prescriptions in a hospital.
A formal process where a patient receives clear information about a proposed treatment or procedure and voluntarily signs their agreement.
A legal medical order instructing healthcare providers not to attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if the patient's breathing or heartbeat stops.
Inflammation or infection of the middle ear air-filled space behind the eardrum.
Bleeding from the nose, commonly originating from Kiesselbach's plexus on the nasal septum.
The perception of ringing, buzzing, roaring, or hissing noise in one or both ears.
Inflammation of the back of the throat (pharynx), causing sore throat, dryness, and pain on swallowing.
Inflammation of the larynx (voice box) from overuse, irritation, or infection, leading to voice hoarseness.
Inflammation and swelling of the tissues lining the sinuses, causing facial pain, nasal congestion, and headache.
Clouding of the eye's natural clear crystalline lens, resulting in blurry, faded, or dimmed vision.
A group of eye conditions that damage the optic nerve, often caused by abnormally high pressure inside the eye.
Inflammation or infection of the transparent membrane (conjunctiva) lining eyelids and white eyeball.
Abnormal visual sensitivity and pain in response to bright light exposure.
Involuntary, rhythmic, rapid oscillations of the eyeballs.
Misalignment of the eyes where both eyes do not look at the same object simultaneously (crossed eyes).
Age-related progressive loss of the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects.
Red, raised, intensely itchy skin welts triggered by histamine release in allergic reactions.
A chronic inflammatory skin condition causing dry, red, itchy, and irritated skin patches.
A chronic autoimmune skin disease where rapid cell multiplication causes thick, red skin covered with silvery scales.
The most aggressive form of skin cancer, arising from pigment-producing cells (melanocytes).
A common, potentially serious bacterial infection of the deeper skin layers and subcutaneous tissues.
A painful, swollen, localized collection of pus caused by bacterial infection surrounded by inflamed tissue.
A circumscribed open sore on skin or mucous membrane accompanied by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue.
The medical removal of dead, damaged, infected, or non-viable tissue to improve healing potential.
A surgical instrument used to clamp severed blood vessels and control bleeding during operations.
A tight constricting band applied around a bleeding limb to compress blood vessels and arrest life-threatening hemorrhage.
Placement of a flexible plastic tube through mouth or nose into the trachea to maintain an open airway for breathing.
The scheduled removal of an endotracheal breathing tube once a patient demonstrates adequate spontaneous respiration.
Life-support technology where an automated ventilator machine moves breathable air in and out of lungs.
A surgical procedure creating an opening through the neck into the trachea to facilitate breathing when upper airway is blocked.
A medication (like Albuterol / Salbutamol) that widens the bronchi and bronchioles to decrease airway resistance.
Powerful intravenous medication (e.g. Norepinephrine) that constricts blood vessels to elevate critically low arterial blood pressure in shock.
Medication that alters the force or energy of muscular contractions, particularly myocardial contraction (e.g. Dobutamine).
A substance that induces sedation by reducing irritability or physiological excitement.
Any member of the group of drugs used to achieve relief from pain.
Medication that reduces elevated body temperature in fever (e.g. Paracetamol).
Medication that is effective against vomiting and nausea (e.g. Ondansetron).
Drug that inhibits the physiological effects of histamine, used to treat allergic rhinitis and urticaria (e.g. Cetirizine).
Class of steroid hormones or synthetic drugs (e.g. Prednisolone) providing potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions.
Medication that inhibits the activity of the immune system to prevent organ rejection or control autoimmune diseases.
The formation or presence of a blood clot within a blood vessel.
The sudden blocking of an artery by an embolus (clot, air, fat) carried in the bloodstream from another site.
Stroke caused by an obstruction within an artery supplying blood to the brain.
Stroke caused by the rupture of a weakened blood vessel into surrounding brain parenchyma.
An abnormal localized outward bulging or ballooning of an arterial wall, vulnerable to rupture.
A localized swelling filled with blood resulting from a break in a blood vessel.
A non-elevated subcutaneous hematoma larger than 1 centimeter; a typical bruise.
Small (1 to 2 mm) red or purple spots on the skin or mucous membranes caused by minor hemorrhage from broken capillaries.
A condition of red or purple spots on the skin that do not blanch on applying pressure, measuring 3 to 10 mm.
A bluish or purplish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes caused by deficient oxygenation of blood.
An unusual paleness of the skin and mucous membranes compared with the normal complexion, indicative of anemia or shock.
Profuse, cold, or inappropriate sweating caused by medical crisis (e.g., myocardial infarction, hypoglycemia, or shock).
Complex metabolic syndrome characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass with or without loss of fat mass in advanced chronic illness.
The abnormal accumulation of triglycerides and lipids within hepatocytes (Fatty Liver Disease).
The surgical removal of the diseased gallbladder.
The surgical excision of the vermiform appendix, typically for acute appendicitis.
The abnormal exit of tissue or an organ through the wall of the cavity in which it normally resides.
A surgically created opening of the bowel brought out onto the surface of the abdomen to divert waste.
A flexible silicone tube inserted through the urethra into the urinary bladder, kept in place with an inflated retention balloon.
A flexible tube inserted through the nose, down the esophagus, and into the stomach for enteral feeding or decompression.
A long, thin catheter placed into a large vein (internal jugular, subclavian) to administer concentrated drugs or fluids.
A thin catheter placed into a peripheral artery (radial) to continuously measure real-time blood pressure and draw blood gases.
